kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-01.title: Multiply the fractions
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-01.body:
Half of a third of a quarter is $\frac12\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac14 = \frac1{24}$ of a day. A day has 24 hours, so this is 1 hour.

**Answer: (E) 1**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-01.title: Work backwards from 24 hours
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-01.body:
A quarter of 24 hours is 6 hours, a third of that is 2 hours, and half of that is 1 hour.

**Answer: (E) 1**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-02.title: Add the pieces
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-02.body:
The path is $AB + BC + CD + DE + EF + FG$. The segments $AB$, $CD$, $EF$ and $FG$ are each a full edge (or parallel to an edge across a face), so each is 12 cm. $BC$ and $DE$ are parallel pieces on the front face that together span its width: $BC + DE = 12$ cm. Total: $4\cdot12 + 12 = 60$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 60 cm**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-03.title: Use the angle sum
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-03.body:
Let $\angle B = x$. Then $\angle A = 3x$ and $\angle C = 2\cdot3x = 6x$. The angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$: $x + 3x + 6x = 10x = 180^\circ$, so $x = 18^\circ$ and $\angle A = 54^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $54^\circ$**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-07.title: Percent of a percent
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-07.body:
30% of 50% of the students is $0.3\cdot0.5 = 0.15$ of the students, i.e. 15%.

**Answer: (A) 15%**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-07.title: Use 100 students
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-07.body:
Of 100 students, 50 swim, and 30% of those 50 is 15 students on the team — 15% of the school.

**Answer: (A) 15%**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-08.title: Parity
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-08.body:
$2n^2$ is always even, and even + odd is odd, so $2n^2 + 2011$ is odd for every $n$.

The others fail: for even $n$, $2011n$, $n^3$ and $n + 2012$ are even; for odd $n$, $n^2 + 2011$ is odd + odd = even.

**Answer: (E) $2n^2 + 2011$**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-08.title: Test n = 0 and n = 1
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-08.body:
With $n = 0$: $0, 2011, 0, 2012, 2011$ — A, C and D are even. With $n = 1$: B gives $2012$, even. Only E remains, and it is always odd because $2n^2$ is even.

**Answer: (E) $2n^2 + 2011$**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-13.title: Angles at A
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-13.body:
The five triangles have total angle sum $5\cdot180^\circ = 900^\circ$. Their angles at $A$ are not marked. The lines through $A$ make vertical (opposite) angles: each angle at $A$ inside a triangle is opposite an equal angle at $A$ that lies outside the triangles, and these 10 angles fill the full $360^\circ$ around $A$. So the triangles' angles at $A$ add up to $180^\circ$.

The 10 marked angles add up to $900^\circ - 180^\circ = 720^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $720^\circ$**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-14.title: Is today a truthful day?
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0708-14.body:
Today Charles either tells the truth (all four statements true) or lies (all four false).

- C is true ($288 = 12\cdot24$) and D is false (he lies on some days).
- Suppose he tells the truth today. Then D was not said, so he said A, B, C and E, all true. By B the number of his friends is even, and by A it is prime, so he has exactly 2 friends — but then E (three friends older than him) is impossible. Contradiction.
- So he lies today, all four statements are false, and the true statement C is the one he did not say. (A, B, D, E can all be false at once, so this works.)

**Answer: (C)**
